# Branches

## Why branch?

A [branch]{.uwred} is a parallel line of work inside one repository. It lets you try something without touching your main version.

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Branches are useful when you want to:

- [Experiment]{.uwred} with a risky change while keeping a working version safe
- Draft a feature that isn't ready for everyone yet
- Keep [`main`]{.uwred} stable while work is in progress

<div class="gap-md"></div>

You've been on a branch the whole time — the default one, called `main`. Now we'll make a second.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Where you are now

List the branches in your repo:

```bash
git branch
```

```
* main
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

The [`*`]{.uwred} (shown in color) marks the branch you're currently on. There's only one so far, and `git status` reminds you of it too (`On branch main`).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Bucky wants to experiment

Bucky is tempted to add a vegetarian spread to the menu — but he doesn't want to disturb the plan that already works.

<div class="gap-md"></div>

Perfect job for a branch: he can draft the veggie options off to the side, decide if he likes them, and only then bring them into `main`.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Create and switch in one step

Make a new branch and move onto it:

```bash
git switch -c veggie-option
```

```
Switched to a new branch 'veggie-option'
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

The [`-c`]{.uwred} flag creates the branch and switches to it. It starts as an exact copy of `main`'s history.

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Confirm where you are:

```bash
git branch
```

```
  main
* veggie-option
```

::: {.footer}
To create a branch without switching, use `git branch <name>`. In older Git, `git checkout -b` does what `git switch -c` does here.
:::


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Work on the branch

Draft the vegetarian items in a new file:

```bash
nano veggie.txt
```

```
Grilled veggie skewers
Portobello "brats" for the vegetarians
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Save it to history as usual — this commit lands on `veggie-option`, not `main`:

```bash
git add veggie.txt
git commit -m "Draft vegetarian options"
```


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## `main` is untouched

Switch back and look:

```bash
git switch main
ls
```

```
brats.txt  cheese_curds.txt  desserts.txt
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

No `veggie.txt` here — it lives only on the branch. [`main` is exactly as you left it.]{.uwred} That isolation is the whole point of branching.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## See the branches diverge

A decorated, graphed log shows how the branches relate:

```bash
git log --oneline --all --graph
```

```
* 7a1b2c3 (veggie-option) Draft vegetarian options
* 1d2e3f4 (HEAD -> main) Ignore scratch files and receipts
* c3d4e5f Add cheese curds and desserts
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

[`--all`]{.uwred} shows every branch and [`--graph`]{.uwred} draws the structure. Here `veggie-option` sits one commit ahead of `main`.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Keep it? Merge into `main`

Bucky likes the veggie options, so he brings them into `main`. First be on the branch you're merging [into]{.uwred}, then merge:

```bash
git switch main
git merge veggie-option
```

```
Updating 1d2e3f4..7a1b2c3
Fast-forward
 veggie.txt | 2 ++
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+)
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

`main` had no new commits of its own, so Git just fast-forwards it to catch up. `veggie.txt` is now part of `main`.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Clean up the branch

Once a branch is merged, delete it to keep things tidy:

```bash
git branch -d veggie-option
```

```
Deleted branch veggie-option (was 7a1b2c3).
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

If a branch is [not]{.uwred} fully merged, `-d` refuses and warns you — so you don't lose work by accident. `git branch -D` (capital D) force-deletes when you really mean it.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## When merges collide

Our merge was clean because `main` hadn't changed. But if `main` and your branch both edited the [same line]{.uwred}, Git can't fast-forward — the merge stops with a [conflict]{.uwred}.

<div class="gap-md"></div>

You already know how to handle it: open the file, remove the `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>` markers, keep what you want, then `git add` and `git commit`. (See the Conflicts unit.)


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Your turn

::: {.callout-wide}
::: {.callout-important}
# Try it
Branch, work, merge, clean up:

1. From `main`, run `git switch -c dessert-upgrade`
2. Add a line to `desserts.txt`, then `git add` and `git commit`
3. `git switch main` and confirm the change isn't there yet
4. `git merge dessert-upgrade`, then `git branch -d dessert-upgrade`
:::
:::


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Where we are

Branches let you work in parallel safely:

- [`git branch`]{.uwred} lists branches; [`git switch -c <name>`]{.uwred} creates and moves onto one
- Commits land on the [current]{.uwred} branch, leaving `main` safe
- [`git merge <branch>`]{.uwred} brings the work together; [`git branch -d`]{.uwred} cleans up

<div class="gap-md"></div>

::: {.callout-wide}
::: {.callout-important}
# Keep going
On GitHub, branches power [pull requests]{.uwred} — the standard way to propose and review changes with collaborators. That's a great next thing to explore, with the [cheatsheet]{.uwred} at your side.
:::
:::
